title: First-Principles Turbulence-Driven Deflagration-to-Detonation Transition Mechanism for Near-Chandrasekhar Mass White Dwarf Progenitors
summary: Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) play an important role throughout astrophysics, most notably as standardizable cosmological candles. Yet, their stellar progenitors and explosion mechanism remain areas of active investigation. For decades, the canonical model for normal brightness SNe Ia used in cosmology was a carbon-oxygen white dwarf (WD) accreting from a non-degenerate stellar companion, approaching the Chandrasekhar mass (M_Ch). Previously, all models of near-M_Ch SNe Ia invoked an ad hoc assumption on the critical process of detonation initiation, and could therefore be tuned to a variety of outcomes. Here, we present global 3D hydrodynamical simulations of near-M_Ch progenitors, which incorporate, for the first time, a laboratory-validated ab initio mechanism for the turbulence-driven deflagration-to-detonation transition (tDDT). The tDDT detonation mechanism is highly efficient, leading to detonation initiation which is prompt in comparison to most prior work. Despite spanning a factor of six in central ignition density and qualitatively distinct ignition topologies, all models converge on nearly identical synthetic spectra at peak luminosity, spectroscopically matched to the overluminous SN 1999aa. The turbulence-driven Chapman-Jouguet criterion drives each progenitor to a common detonation configuration from diverse initial conditions, providing a physical foundation for the ignition-insensitive detonation outcomes implicit in the empirical standardizability of SNe Ia. This provides the first physically motivated, self-consistent pathway for delayed detonation in SNe Ia simulations. Further work is necessary to understand how this mechanism might produce more delayed detonation initiation and potentially fail, thereby yielding SNe Iax.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first global 3D hydrodynamical simulations of near-Chandrasekhar mass Type Ia supernovae incorporating a laboratory-validated ab initio turbulence-driven deflagration-to-detonation transition (tDDT) mechanism. The simulations show that despite diverse initial conditions, all models converge on nearly identical synthetic spectra matching SN 1999aa, providing a physical foundation for the empirical standardizability of SNe Ia.
AI.motivation: SNe Ia are critical as standardizable cosmological candles, but their progenitor systems and explosion mechanisms remain poorly understood. Prior near-M_Ch models relied on ad hoc assumptions about detonation initiation, lacking a physically grounded mechanism.
AI.method: Global 3D hydrodynamical simulations of near-M_Ch carbon-oxygen white dwarf progenitors incorporating a laboratory-validated ab initio tDDT mechanism, tested across a factor of six in central ignition density and qualitatively distinct ignition topologies.
AI.result: The tDDT mechanism is highly efficient, producing prompt detonation initiation. All models converge on nearly identical synthetic spectra at peak luminosity, spectroscopically matched to the overluminous SN 1999aa, despite diverse initial conditions.
AI.conclusion: The turbulence-driven Chapman-Jouguet criterion drives progenitors to a common detonation configuration, providing a physical basis for the ignition-insensitive detonation outcomes underlying SNe Ia standardizability. This is the first physically motivated, self-consistent delayed detonation pathway. Further work is needed to explore how this mechanism might produce more delayed initiation or fail (yielding SNe Iax).

title: Gravitational wave detectability range informed by external messengers
summary: A rapid estimate of gravitational-wave (GW) detectability associated with astronomical transients is crucial for optimizing multi-messenger follow-up strategies and for constraining the physical origin of the transient itself. We introduce here the Targeted Detectability Range (TDR), designed to evaluate with minimal computational effort the detectability of compact binary coalescences under the hypothesis of association with an external messenger, such as an electromagnetic or neutrino signal. Unlike the standard GW range, which is based on averaged source parameters, the TDR incorporates prior information from observations of the external messenger, including sky localization, inclination constraints, and physically motivated bounds on component masses. We report the detectability range of all gamma-ray bursts, short and long duration, observed during the first three observing runs of the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration. The method is validated by performing a systematic comparison with the 90$\%$ exclusion distances provided by modeled targeted GW searches.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Targeted Detectability Range (TDR), a computationally efficient method for estimating gravitational-wave detectability of compact binary coalescences associated with external messengers (e.g., electromagnetic or neutrino signals), using prior information from the messenger to improve upon the standard GW range. The method is validated against gamma-ray bursts from LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA's first three observing runs.
AI.motivation: To provide a rapid, computationally minimal estimate of GW detectability for astronomical transients associated with external messengers, enabling optimized multi-messenger follow-up strategies and better constraints on the physical origin of transients.
AI.method: The authors propose the Targeted Detectability Range (TDR), which incorporates prior information from external messengers (sky localization, inclination constraints, mass bounds) into detectability estimates, unlike the standard GW range that uses averaged source parameters. They validate TDR against modeled targeted GW searches using gamma-ray burst data from LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA's first three observing runs.
AI.result: The TDR provides detectability ranges for all gamma-ray bursts (short and long duration) observed during the first three observing runs of LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA. Systematic comparison with 90% exclusion distances from modeled targeted GW searches confirms the method's validity.
AI.conclusion: The TDR offers a computationally efficient and validated approach for estimating GW detectability in multi-messenger contexts, improving upon standard range methods by incorporating external messenger priors.

title: Massquerade: Impacts of Mass Ratio Reversals on Binary Black Hole Merger Rates and Mass Distributions
summary: We investigate the role of mass ratio reversal (MRR), in which the initially less massive star in a binary forms the more massive compact object, in shaping the astrophysical binary black hole (BBH) merger rate and mass distribution inferred by LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA, comparing simulation outcomes from population synthesis frameworks COMPAS and SEVN. We find that the observational imprint of MRR differs qualitatively between the two models. In COMPAS, MRR systems dominate the merger rate density at high primary masses ( $\gtrsim$ 12 M$_\odot$), high secondary masses ( $\gtrsim$ 20 M$_\odot$), and high mass ratios ($q>0.6$), whereas in SEVN, MRR systems remain subdominant across the BBH mass distribution. This implies that the initially less massive star can massquerade as the observed primary black hole, such that the primary-mass distribution is not a direct tracer of the initially more massive stars, but instead a superposition of physically distinct evolutionary populations. We identify in the simulations three distinct evolutionary pathways leading to MRR systems: core-growth, in which stable mass transfer increases the helium-core mass of the secondary; PPISN-shrinking, where pulsational pair-instability episodes reduce the primary remnant mass; and asymmetric-CCSN, where differential supernova mass loss drives the reversal. When weighted by the local BBH merger-rate density, the core-growth channel dominates almost exclusively. MRR systems predominantly originate from massive ($\gtrsim$ 50 M$_\odot$), low-metallicity progenitors, with most of the systems forming below 0.1 $Z_\odot$. Our results demonstrate that MRR is a physically distinct and potentially observable feature of isolated binary evolution. Accounting for MRR will be important for robustly connecting future gravitational-wave observations to the physics of massive binary evolution and compact-object formation.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates mass ratio reversal (MRR) in binary black hole mergers using two population synthesis codes (COMPAS and SEVN), finding that MRR significantly shapes the observed BBH mass distribution, with distinct predictions between the two models. Three evolutionary pathways for MRR are identified, with the core-growth channel dominating when weighted by merger-rate density.
AI.motivation: To understand how mass ratio reversal (MRR)—where the initially less massive star becomes the more massive compact object—influences the astrophysical binary black hole merger rate and mass distribution observed by LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA, and to determine whether MRR leaves observable imprints that could be detected in gravitational-wave data.
AI.method: The authors compare simulation outcomes from two population synthesis frameworks: COMPAS and SEVN. They analyze the contribution of MRR systems to the BBH merger rate density across primary mass, secondary mass, and mass ratio. They identify distinct evolutionary pathways (core-growth, PPISN-shrinking, asymmetric-CCSN) and trace progenitor properties such as initial mass and metallicity.
AI.result: MRR imprints differ qualitatively between COMPAS and SEVN: COMPAS predicts MRR dominance at high primary masses (>12 M☉), high secondary masses (>20 M☉), and high mass ratios (q>0.6), while SEVN shows MRR subdominant across the BBH mass distribution. Three pathways are identified, with core-growth dominating. MRR systems arise from massive (>50 M☉), low-metallicity (<0.1 Z☉) progenitors.
AI.conclusion: MRR is a physically distinct and potentially observable feature of isolated binary evolution. The initially less massive star can masquerade as the observed primary black hole, meaning the primary-mass distribution is a superposition of distinct evolutionary populations rather than a direct tracer of initially more massive stars. Accounting for MRR will be crucial for robustly connecting gravitational-wave observations to massive binary evolution and compact-object formation physics.

title: A Generalized Template Matching Algorithm for Correcting Jitter Noise in Pulsar Timing
summary: Pulsar timing is a valuable source of high-precision astrophysical measurements which can be used to probe gravitational physics, including by detecting gravitational waves. An important factor limiting the precision of these measurements is pulse jitter; i.e., intrinsic, short-timescale variation in the amplitude and shape of pulses from a given pulsar. Because conventional pulse time-of-arrival (TOA) measurement relies on template matching, which assumes the average pulse shape is stable, such variation gives rise to jitter noise in TOA measurements. Here we introduce a generalization of the template matching technique, making use of principal component analysis, which can account for variations in pulse shape. We compare this technique to other proposals for mitigating jitter noise in pulsar timing, paying particular attention to the possibility of corrections absorbing other astrophysical signals of interest, and demonstrate its effectiveness using simulated data.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a generalized template matching technique using principal component analysis to account for pulse shape variations in pulsar timing, reducing jitter noise that limits measurement precision, and demonstrates its effectiveness on simulated data while comparing to other mitigation proposals.
AI.motivation: Pulse jitter (intrinsic short-timescale variation in pulse amplitude and shape) limits the precision of pulsar timing measurements, which are valuable for probing gravitational physics including gravitational wave detection.
AI.method: The authors generalize the conventional template matching technique by incorporating principal component analysis (PCA) to account for variations in pulse shape, rather than assuming a stable average pulse shape.
AI.result: The technique demonstrates effectiveness on simulated data, and the authors compare it to other proposals for mitigating jitter noise while paying attention to the risk of corrections absorbing other astrophysical signals of interest.
AI.conclusion: The PCA-based generalized template matching offers a promising approach to reduce jitter noise in pulsar timing measurements, potentially improving the precision of astrophysical measurements including gravitational wave detection.

title: (LRDs)$^2$: The Low-ReDshift Little Red Dots Survey. II. DESI DR1 Sample
comment: Main text 28 pages; 17 figures. Submitted to the ApJ. Comments are welcome. Data are available on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20309303
summary: JWST has revealed a substantial population of "Little Red Dots" (LRDs) at $z>4$, challenging conventional AGN frameworks. However, the low-redshift regime remains largely unexplored. In the second paper of the (LRDs)$^2$ series, we present a systematic selection from DESI DR1 and identify 27 LRDs at $z=0.2-0.9$, yielding a number density lower limit of $7.5 \times 10^{-10}$ cMpc$^{-3}$. We conducted near-IR spectroscopic follow-up observations for 18 of them, revealing their full SED shapes and emission lines. These low-$z$ LRDs share the hallmark properties of their high-$z$ counterparts: compact morphology, V-shaped UV-optical continua, broad Balmer emission with extreme decrements (median H$α$/H$β\sim 16$), frequent Balmer absorption (67%), and blackbody-like optical-to-near-IR continua. All have low metallicity, occupy the same regions in the BPT diagram as high-$z$ LRDs, and have softer ionizing spectra than typical AGNs. The consistency between low-$z$ and high-$z$ LRD properties indicates the same physical processes at work. The correlation between broad-line Balmer luminosity and $L_{5100}$ deviates from that of local type-1 AGNs, limiting the direct application of local BH mass calibrations. Ionized [O III] outflows are ubiquitous (78%). One LRD at $z=0.196$, J1717+3807, shows robust long-term variability in $i$ and WISE bands. The optical-to-NIR continua of LRDs reveal a wide range of temperatures $\sim 2000-4700$ K (peak $0.6-1.5$ $μ$m), with a subset showing cooler and larger envelopes than those at high $z$. Low-$z$ LRDs serve not only as proximate laboratories for probing the nature of LRDs, but also trace the cosmic evolution of this population from the cosmic dawn to the present day.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies 27 "Little Red Dots" (LRDs) at z=0.2-0.9 from DESI DR1, with spectroscopic follow-up for 18 objects. Low-z LRDs share key properties with their high-z counterparts (compact morphology, V-shaped continua, broad Balmer lines with extreme decrements, Balmer absorption, low metallicity), confirming the same physical processes. They deviate from local AGN scaling relations, show ubiquitous ionized outflows, and exhibit diverse dust temperatures (2000-4700 K). One LRD (J1717+3807) shows long-term variability.
AI.motivation: While JWST has revealed abundant LRDs at z>4, the low-redshift regime remains largely unexplored. This study aims to fill that gap to test whether LRDs exist locally and share the same physical nature as their high-z counterparts.
AI.method: Systematic selection from DESI DR1, identifying 27 LRDs at z=0.2-0.9, with near-IR spectroscopic follow-up for 18 objects to characterize SED shapes, emission lines, and physical properties.
AI.result: 27 LRDs identified with number density >7.5e-10 cMpc^{-3}. They show V-shaped UV-optical continua, broad Balmer emission with extreme Hα/Hβ~16, 67% Balmer absorption, low metallicity, BPT diagram consistency with high-z LRDs, softer ionizing spectra than typical AGNs, ubiquitous [O III] outflows (78%), and diverse blackbody-like continua (2000-4700 K). The broad-line luminosity-L5100 relation deviates from local type-1 AGNs.
AI.conclusion: Low-z and high-z LRDs share consistent properties, indicating the same physical processes. Low-z LRDs serve as proximate laboratories for understanding LRD nature and trace cosmic evolution of this population from cosmic dawn to present day.

title: The powerful shocks in RS Oph: NuSTAR X-ray data and a complete review
comment: Accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal
summary: In the 2021 outburst of RS Ophiuchi, the gamma- and the X-ray flux were measured quasi-simultaneously from day 1 after the optical peak, offering the first comprehensive view of shocks in a nova occurring in a symbiotic system. We present a previously unpublished observation done with NuSTAR in the 3-79 keV range, 9 days after maximum, and we review the complex history of the evidence of shocks in the previous outbursts of this nova in the light of the intensive X-ray monitoring of 2021. We find evidence that the shock causing the particle acceleration measured with the Cherenkov telescopes produced also the thermal flux detected in the 0.2-30 keV X-ray range, while the large gamma-ray flux observed with Fermi after about a day, is not consistent with the X-ray observations. We conclude that an initial, strong shock, with particle-particle loss timescale shorter than the timescale of particle acceleration at energy higher than a few GeV, occurred close to the red giant atmosphere,where either the X-rays' emitting volume was reduced by turbulence, or - perhaps less likely - the X-rays were completely absorbed by large column density near the giant and by the accretion wake along the line of sight. We compare RS Oph with other novae in long period systems with evolved companions,discussing how the shocks' phenomenology is a powerful tool to derive other physical parameters. Finally, we discuss predictions that in T CrB, expected to have a new outburst within the next few years, the shocks may not be as energetic as in RS Oph.

AI.tldr: Analysis of quasi-simultaneous gamma-ray and X-ray observations of the 2021 RS Ophiuchi nova outburst reveals that the shock causing particle acceleration (detected by Cherenkov telescopes) also produced the thermal X-ray flux, but the early Fermi gamma-ray emission is inconsistent with X-ray data, suggesting an initial strong shock near the red giant where X-rays were either turbulence-reduced or absorbed.
AI.motivation: To understand the complex shock physics in symbiotic novae by leveraging the first quasi-simultaneous gamma-ray and X-ray measurements from the 2021 RS Oph outburst, and to compare with previous outbursts to derive physical parameters.
AI.method: Analysis of a previously unpublished NuSTAR observation (3-79 keV, day 9 post-maximum) combined with review of prior X-ray monitoring data and comparison with gamma-ray observations from Fermi and Cherenkov telescopes.
AI.result: The shock causing Cherenkov-detected particle acceleration also produced the thermal X-ray flux (0.2-30 keV), but the early Fermi gamma-ray flux (day ~1) is inconsistent with X-ray observations, implying an initial strong shock near the red giant atmosphere with either reduced X-ray emitting volume via turbulence or absorption by high column density and accretion wake.
AI.conclusion: Shock phenomenology is a powerful diagnostic for deriving physical parameters in symbiotic novae; predictions for T CrB suggest its future outburst may feature less energetic shocks than RS Oph.

title: Investigating central star formation in local AGN host galaxies: is there tension between coeval growth and AGN feedback?
comment: 15 pages, 17 figures. Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: It has been argued that supermassive black holes (BHs) coevolve with the central parts of galaxies, as a result of the common fuel for both the BH and star formation in the galaxy central region, as supported by the particularly significant relation between BH growth and the central mass density within 1 kpc found among star-forming galaxies. In the context of this scenario, one would naturally expect a close observational link between AGN activity and star formation activity in the central regions, e.g., the surface star formation rate density in the central 1 kpc region ($Σ_{\rm SFR, 1~kpc}$), as the manifestation of coeval growth. With ~3000 galaxies in the Mapping Nearby Galaxies at Apache Point Observatory (MaNGA) survey that have X-ray coverage from SRG/eROSITA, XMM-Newton, or Chandra, we studied how the X-ray AGN fraction varies with $Σ_{\rm SFR, 1~kpc}$. We found that the fraction of X-ray AGNs with relatively higher specific BH accretion rates increases with $Σ_{\rm SFR, 1~kpc}$, consistent with the expectation. Comparison of the mean star formation rate surface density ($Σ_{\rm SFR}$) profiles of the host galaxies of these AGNs and normal galaxies sharing similar properties reveals elevated $Σ_{\rm SFR}$ in AGN hosts across the entire central region. As for optically-selected AGNs, their hosts also tend to show high $Σ_{\rm SFR}$ in the central regions on average compared to normal galaxies, but are discrepant with X-ray AGNs in terms of the trend of AGN fraction vs. $Σ_{\rm SFR, 1~kpc}$, which can be explained by selection effects. While these general trends all support the coeval growth scenario, they do not contradict observational evidence for AGN feedback, as the time-averaged effects from local AGN feedback are modest in star-forming regions.

AI.tldr: Using ~3,000 MaNGA galaxies with X-ray data, this study finds that X-ray AGN fraction increases with central star formation rate density (ΣSFR, 1 kpc), supporting the coevolution scenario of supermassive black holes and their host galaxies, while optical AGN selection effects cause discrepancies.
AI.motivation: To test the coevolution scenario between supermassive black holes and their host galaxies by examining the observational link between AGN activity and central star formation rate density, motivated by the known relation between BH growth and central mass density within 1 kpc in star-forming galaxies.
AI.method: Analyzed ~3,000 galaxies from the MaNGA survey with X-ray coverage from SRG/eROSITA, XMM-Newton, or Chandra. Computed the X-ray AGN fraction as a function of ΣSFR, 1 kpc, compared mean ΣSFR profiles of AGN hosts vs. normal galaxies, and contrasted results with optically-selected AGNs.
AI.result: X-ray AGN fraction with higher specific BH accretion rates increases with ΣSFR, 1 kpc. AGN hosts show elevated ΣSFR across the entire central region compared to normal galaxies. Optically-selected AGNs also show high central ΣSFR but exhibit different trends in AGN fraction vs. ΣSFR, 1 kpc due to selection effects.
AI.conclusion: The results support the coeval growth scenario for BHs and galaxies, while not contradicting AGN feedback evidence, as local feedback effects are modest in star-forming regions when time-averaged.

title: Self-Supervised ConvLSTM for Fermi Large Area Telescope Transient Detection
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures. Accepted for publication in Astronomy and Computing. Author-accepted manuscript version
summary: We present a framework for detecting transient gamma-ray phenomena in a controlled environment by combining end-to-end simulations of the Fermi-LAT sky with self-supervised spatio-temporal deep learning. We generate a ten-year synthetic Universe with gtobssim and process the simulated events into daily all-sky maps of counts and exposure, obtaining a time-ordered sequence that mirrors the structure of Fermi-LAT observations. To model the nominal evolution of the sky, we employ a Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory (ConvLSTM) network that operates directly on map sequences, preserving spatial locality while learning temporal dependencies. The model is trained to reconstruct expected emission, and departures from the learned baseline are quantified through pixel-wise mean-squared residual maps. We then define statistically motivated anomaly criteria by estimating per-pixel thresholds from the residual distribution on the training set, and we enforce spatial coherence via local filtering to suppress isolated fluctuations. The ConvLSTM is then deployed as trained predictor on Fermi-LAT daily maps, where the sky can depart from the nominal behavior because of genuine astrophysical variability and instrumental non-stationarities. The resulting pipeline flags localized, time-dependent excesses consistent with high-variable sources or transient events (e.g., flares or GRBs) and provides a benchmark for evaluating anomaly-detection strategies on long-duration, Fermi-LAT-like datasets.

AI.tldr: A framework combining end-to-end simulations of the Fermi-LAT sky with self-supervised spatio-temporal deep learning (ConvLSTM) to detect transient gamma-ray phenomena by learning nominal sky evolution and flagging anomalous excesses.
AI.motivation: To detect transient gamma-ray phenomena (e.g., flares, GRBs) in a controlled, data-driven manner by modeling the nominal sky evolution and identifying statistically significant departures from it.
AI.method: Generate a ten-year synthetic Fermi-LAT sky using gtobssim, process into daily all-sky count/exposure maps, train a ConvLSTM to reconstruct expected emission, compute pixel-wise mean-squared residuals, define per-pixel anomaly thresholds from residual distributions, apply spatial coherence filtering, and deploy on real Fermi-LAT daily data.
AI.result: The pipeline flags localized, time-dependent excesses consistent with high-variable sources or transient events, providing a benchmark for anomaly-detection strategies on long-duration gamma-ray datasets.
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised spatio-temporal deep learning on simulated Fermi-LAT data can effectively detect transient gamma-ray phenomena, offering a principled anomaly detection strategy for Fermi-LAT-like observations.

title: Decomposing cool stellar populations with H-band spectral fluctuations: Long-period variable stars in NGC 5128 and carbon stars in NGC 5102
summary: We analyse new H-band integral-field unit observations of two galaxies at ~4 Mpc, using a principal components analysis of pixel spectra to probe their giant star content. In both galaxies, the signals arise in near-resolved point-like sources without large-scale variation, consistent with each pixel sampling stars randomly from a common underlying population. In the (mostly) old bulge of NGC 5128, the observed pixel-to-pixel variation is dominated by a component with a mid-M giant spectrum with prominent CO bandheads. We also recover a smoother second spectral component, apparently driven by contributions from later spectral types. This component is not present in predictions from Poisson-sampled models of old stellar populations; we suggest that it arises from the cool phases of long-period variable stars. (An appendix provides direct evidence for such variables in complementary two-epoch MUSE observations.) In the contrasting galaxy NGC 5102, where a post-starburst stellar population is known to be present, we again find two distinct components. As before, the first component carries the CO bands typical of M-giants. The second eigenspectrum in this younger galaxy shows a strong 1.77 micron C2 bandhead, a feature which is characteristic of carbon stars. Our results highlight the ability of integral field data to access information beyond the total spectrum, even when individual stars cannot be classically resolved.

AI.tldr: The paper uses H-band IFU observations of two nearby galaxies (~4 Mpc) and PCA of pixel spectra to probe their giant star content. In NGC 5128 (old bulge), pixel variation is dominated by mid-M giants with a second component from long-period variable stars. In NGC 5102 (post-starburst), the second component shows a strong C2 bandhead from carbon stars. The study demonstrates IFU data can reveal stellar population information beyond the integrated spectrum, even without resolving individual stars.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that integral-field unit (IFU) spectroscopy can reveal detailed information about the giant star content of nearby galaxies beyond what is accessible from integrated spectra, even when individual stars remain classically unresolved.
AI.method: Principal components analysis (PCA) of pixel spectra from H-band IFU observations of two galaxies at ~4 Mpc (NGC 5128 and NGC 5102), supplemented by two-epoch MUSE observations for variable star identification.
AI.result: In NGC 5128 (old bulge), pixel variation is dominated by mid-M giant spectra with prominent CO bandheads, plus a smoother second component attributed to cool phases of long-period variable stars. In NGC 5102 (post-starburst), the first component shows M-giant CO bands while the second eigenspectrum exhibits a strong 1.77 μm C2 bandhead characteristic of carbon stars.
AI.conclusion: IFU observations enable access to stellar population information beyond the total integrated spectrum even when individual stars cannot be classically resolved, revealing distinct giant star populations and their variability in nearby galaxies.

title: A Magnetized Black Hole Envelope Model for Little Red Dots
summary: Recent observations have revealed a unique class of active galactic nuclei (AGNs), termed little red dots (LRDs). These objects are hypothesized to be powered by massive black holes rapidly accreting in dense gaseous environments. Theoretical studies suggest that the circum-nuclear gas can form an optically thick black hole envelope (BHE), whose structure resembles the atmospheres of convective stars near the Hayashi limit. Given that such cool stars typically generate magnetic fields, we propose a dynamical and spectral model for an LRD enshrouded by a magnetized BHE. Assuming spherical free-fall accretion onto a rotating, magnetized BHE, our model accounts for key observational properties of LRDs. We propose that the Doppler component of broad emission lines originates from plasma clumps co-rotating within the BHE magnetosphere. Including additional broadening due to electron scattering allows the resulting line profile to be fitted by a combination of a Gaussian core and an exponential tail. This model can reproduce Doppler components up to a few thousand ${\rm km~s^{-1}}$. We suggest that conventional black hole mass estimation methods based on the virial relation may yield erroneous results. Furthermore, our model is consistent with X-ray non-detections in LRDs. We evaluate the X-ray luminosities of two potential sources: the post-shock region of accretion shocks and a magnetically heated corona. We find that these X-ray luminosities are constrained to $\lesssim 10^{41}~{\rm erg~s^{-1}}$ across a wide range of black hole masses ($10^5 M_\odot \lesssim M_{\rm BH}\lesssim 10^7M_\odot$) and accretion rates, consistent with current upper limits on X-ray emission.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a magnetized black hole envelope (BHE) model to explain little red dots (LRDs) — a unique class of AGNs. Using spherical free-fall accretion onto a rotating, magnetized BHE, the model explains broad emission line Doppler components (up to thousands of km/s) via co-rotating plasma clumps, predicts X-ray non-detections (<10^41 erg/s) across a wide black hole mass range (10^5-10^7 M⊙), and cautions that standard virial black hole mass estimates may be misleading for LRDs.
AI.motivation: To explain the observational properties of little red dots (LRDs), a newly discovered class of AGNs characterized by rapid accretion in dense gaseous environments, by proposing a theoretical model that addresses their broad emission lines, X-ray non-detections, and potential biases in black hole mass estimation.
AI.method: The authors develop a dynamical and spectral model assuming spherical free-fall accretion onto a rotating, magnetized black hole envelope (BHE). They treat the BHE as analogous to convective star atmospheres near the Hayashi limit, incorporate magnetospheric plasma clumps to generate broad emission lines via Doppler shifts and electron scattering broadening, and evaluate X-ray luminosities from accretion shocks and magnetically heated coronae.
AI.result: The model reproduces Doppler components up to a few thousand km/s, explains broad emission line profiles as a combination of Gaussian core and exponential tail, predicts X-ray luminosities ≤10^41 erg/s across BH masses 10^5-10^7 M⊙ and various accretion rates, and suggests that virial-based BH mass estimates may be erroneous for LRDs.
AI.conclusion: A magnetized BHE model can self-consistently account for multiple LRD observational features including broad line widths, X-ray weakness, and potential mass estimation biases, providing a unified theoretical framework for this enigmatic AGN class.

title: Quasi-Simultaneous Broadband Spectral Energy Distributions of a Sample of Fermi Blazars -- I. Correlation Results
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables, accepted for publication by MNRAS
summary: Blazars' non-thermal emission shows rapid variability across all wavelengths, so spectral energy distributions (SEDs) built from quasi-simultaneous data are crucial for revealing the jets physical properties. In this work, we construct quasi-simultaneous broadband SEDs for 93 Fermi blazars (56 FSRQs, 35 BL Lacs, and 2 blazar candidates of uncertain type), fit both peaks with cubic functions to allow for potential asymmetries, and examine correlations among key parameters. Our main results are summarized as follows: (1) We find that synchrotron peak frequency and curvature are only weakly related, suggesting that charged particles are accelerated by mixed acceleration mechanism. (2) The blazar sequence is confirmed in the observer's frame through negative correlations of both the bolometic luminosity $\log L_{\rm bol}$ and the Compton dominance $\log Y$ with the synchrotron peak frequency $\log ν_{\rm syn}^{\rm peak}$. After correcting for Doppler boosting, a weak positive correlation emerges between $\log L_{\rm bol}$ and $\log ν_{\rm syn}^{\rm peak}$. FSRQs and BL Lacs exhibit distinct correlation patterns within the blazar sequence, indicating differences in cooling mechanisms. (3) Using variability time lags between 0.1-1 GeV and 1-300 GeV light curves, we estimate lower limits of Doppler factors for 4 sources, providing a jet-speed diagnostic anchored directly to the $γ$-ray emission zone.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes quasi-simultaneous broadband SEDs for 93 Fermi blazars, fitting both peaks with cubic functions. Key findings include: weak correlation between synchrotron peak frequency and curvature suggesting mixed acceleration mechanisms; confirmation of the blazar sequence with negative correlations between luminosity/Compton dominance and peak frequency, with FSRQs and BL Lacs showing distinct cooling patterns; and estimation of Doppler factor lower limits for 4 sources using gamma-ray variability time lags.
AI.motivation: Blazars exhibit rapid multi-wavelength variability, so quasi-simultaneous SEDs are essential for accurately revealing the physical properties of their jets.
AI.method: Constructed quasi-simultaneous broadband SEDs for 93 Fermi blazars (56 FSRQs, 35 BL Lacs, 2 uncertain); fitted both SED peaks with cubic functions to allow asymmetries; examined correlations among key parameters; used variability time lags between 0.1-1 GeV and 1-300 GeV light curves to estimate Doppler factor lower limits.
AI.result: (1) Weak correlation between synchrotron peak frequency and curvature → mixed acceleration mechanisms. (2) Blazar sequence confirmed in observer's frame (negative log L_bol and log Y vs log ν_syn^peak); after Doppler correction, weak positive correlation between log L_bol and log ν_syn^peak; FSRQs and BL Lacs show distinct correlation patterns. (3) Lower limits of Doppler factors derived for 4 sources using gamma-ray variability.
AI.conclusion: The study supports the blazar sequence, reveals acceleration and cooling mechanism differences between FSRQs and BL Lacs, and provides a jet-speed diagnostic tied to the gamma-ray emission zone.

title: Nature of 4FGL J2249.4+6229: Evidence for a redback system with a cool companion and low X-ray and $γ$-ray luminosities
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: We report the identification of the likely X-ray and optical counterpart to the unassociated Fermi source 4FGL J2249.4+6229. To clarify its nature, we investigate the X-ray data from Swift/XRT and SRG/eROSITA as well as photometric data from optical catalogues and archival spectroscopic data from the Gemini-North telescope. Using Zwicky Transient Facility data spanning over 6.6 yr, we confirmed a period of $\approx$5.6 h likely associated with the orbital motion in a binary system. The folded light curves have a smooth sinusoidal shape with two peaks per period and the amplitude of $\approx$0.2 mag. The X-ray spectra of the source are well fitted by an absorbed power law with the photon index of $\approx$2.0 and unabsorbed flux of $\approx$1.4$\times10^{-13}$ erg s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$. All these together with the X-ray to optical flux ratio of $\sim$0.2 implies that 4FGL J2249.4+6229 is a promising redback candidate. Fitting the optical light curves with the direct heating model, we obtained the companion mass of $\approx$0.5 M$_\odot$ and temperature of $\approx$3600 K implying an M-type star. This places it among the coldest and most massive companions known in redback systems.Optical spectra confirms the M-type star and shows the broad asymmetric H$α$ emission line. For the distance of 500--550 pc derived from the optical data, the source can be the redback with the lowest X-ray and $γ$-ray luminosities.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies the likely X-ray and optical counterpart of the unassociated Fermi source 4FGL J2249.4+6229, confirming it as a redback candidate — a binary system with a ≈5.6 h orbital period, an M-type companion star of ≈0.5 M☉ and ≈3600 K, and the lowest X-ray and γ-ray luminosities among known redbacks at a distance of 500–550 pc.
AI.motivation: To clarify the nature of the unassociated Fermi source 4FGL J2249.4+6229 by identifying its X-ray and optical counterpart and determining whether it belongs to the redback class of binary systems.
AI.method: Analysis of X-ray data from Swift/XRT and SRG/eROSITA, optical photometric data from catalogues and Zwicky Transient Facility (6.6 yr baseline), archival spectroscopy from Gemini-North, and fitting with a direct heating model.
AI.result: Confirmed a ≈5.6 h orbital period with double-peaked sinusoidal light curves (amplitude ≈0.2 mag). X-ray spectra fit an absorbed power law (photon index ≈2.0, flux ≈1.4×10⁻¹³ erg s⁻¹ cm⁻²). X-ray-to-optical flux ratio ≈0.2. Companion mass ≈0.5 M☉, temperature ≈3600 K (M-type star). Broad asymmetric Hα emission detected. Distance 500–550 pc implies the lowest X-ray and γ-ray luminosities among known redbacks.
AI.conclusion: 4FGL J2249.4+6229 is a promising redback candidate with the coldest and most massive companion among known systems, and the lowest X-ray and γ-ray luminosities at the inferred distance.

title: Predicting intermediate-mass black hole formation in star clusters with machine learning
summary: Whether intermediate-mass black holes reside in nearby star clusters has remained contested for decades. We address this question by training neural network and random forest regressors on synthetic catalogs generated with the {\sc Rapster} cluster evolution code, mapping observable cluster properties such as total mass and half-mass radius onto the mass of the heaviest black hole built up through repeated mergers. Applying these models to nearby globular and nuclear star clusters, we forecast the intermediate-mass black hole population that each system may host. Globular clusters are unlikely to contain black holes more massive than $\sim 100\,M_\odot$, with an occupation fraction near 0.02, although they can produce remnants within the upper mass gap with masses approaching $100\,M_\odot$. Among nuclear star clusters, a handful of cases, including NGC 5102 and NGC 5206, yield predicted central black hole masses above $100\,M_\odot$, which we contrast with kinematically inferred estimates. Where the observationally claimed masses exceed our predictions, the implication is that the assembly history involved processes beyond hierarchical mergers, most plausibly accretion of gas and stars. Finally, we employ a normalizing flow to quantify, for individual globular clusters, the likelihood that their initial conditions were favorable to a collisional runaway during the first few million years after formation.

AI.tldr: This study uses machine learning regressors (neural networks and random forests) trained on synthetic cluster evolution catalogs to predict black hole masses in star clusters, finding that globular clusters are unlikely to host intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) above ~100 M☉ (occupation fraction ~0.02), while some nuclear star clusters (e.g., NGC 5102, NGC 5206) may harbor IMBHs. Discrepancies with kinematic inferences suggest non-merger assembly channels, and normalizing flows assess collisional runaway likelihood in early cluster evolution.
AI.motivation: The long-standing debate over whether intermediate-mass black holes reside in nearby star clusters motivated the authors to develop predictive models that can infer black hole masses from observable cluster properties.
AI.method: The authors trained neural network and random forest regressors on synthetic catalogs from the Rapster cluster evolution code, mapping observable properties (total mass, half-mass radius) to the mass of the heaviest black hole from repeated mergers. They applied these models to nearby globular and nuclear star clusters and used normalizing flows to quantify collisional runaway likelihood.
AI.result: Globular clusters rarely host black holes >100 M☉ (occupation fraction ~0.02) but can produce remnants in the upper mass gap (~100 M☉). Some nuclear star clusters (NGC 5102, NGC 5206) predict central black hole masses >100 M☉. Discrepancies between predictions and kinematic estimates suggest additional assembly processes beyond hierarchical mergers.
AI.conclusion: Globular clusters are unlikely IMBH hosts, while nuclear star clusters show more promise. Where observational claims exceed predictions, gas/stellar accretion likely plays a role. Normalizing flows provide probabilistic assessments of early collisional runaway scenarios.

title: Magnetar Fireballs and Short Bursts: Curved Spacetime Lensing, QED Effects, High-Energy Spectra and Polarization, and Energy-Time Impulse Responses
summary: Magnetar short bursts (SBs) are hard X-ray transients of durations $0.01-1$ s peaking at $\sim 10-100$ keV, and are prime targets for new high-energy missions and polarimeters. The recent association of SBs with bright radio bursts in SGR 1935+2154 has broadened interest in SB physics. We present new advanced fireball models combining general relativistic light bending, polarized transport in magnetized photospheres, magnetic photon splitting attenuation, and magnetospheric vacuum birefringence. These models also have relevance to trapped fireballs in magnetar giant flare pulsating tails. We adopt confined flux tube geometries consistent with adiabatic fireballs, and anisotropic/polarized emergent intensities to produce spectra and polarizations, and energy-time Stokes impulse responses. We predict that most fireballs are highly linearly polarized, especially when vacuum birefringence is important. There is rich potential for diagnostics: coexisting direct and lensed delayed images, gaps by occultation of the neutron star surface, and Shapiro+Rømer delay with temporal caustics. These effects can imprint spin phase dependence of the spectral and polarization character of bursts. Predicted signatures depend strongly on viewing geometry, fireball configuration, and photon splitting assumptions, yielding large variance in model high-energy spectral shapes and cutoffs, and energy-dependent polarization. The models can reproduce established double-blackbody SB spectral phenomenology, and we find that the unusual April 2020 radio-associated SB from SGR 1935+2154 is broadly consistent with a footpoint close to the magnetic pole, and possibly near pole-on viewing geometry. Our models motivate reverberation-style analyses for SBs and suggest that high-quality data might constrain source geometry, burst crustal footpoints, and, potentially, neutron star masses and radii.

AI.tldr: The paper presents advanced fireball models for magnetar short bursts, incorporating general relativity, polarized transport, photon splitting, and vacuum birefringence. It predicts high linear polarization, spin-phase-dependent spectral and polarization signatures, and demonstrates consistency with the April 2020 radio-associated SB from SGR 1935+2154, suggesting potential constraints on source geometry, footpoint locations, and neutron star masses and radii.
AI.motivation: Magnetar short bursts are hard X-ray transients of interest for new high-energy missions and polarimeters, especially following their association with bright radio bursts in SGR 1935+2154, motivating advanced modeling to understand their physics and diagnostic potential.
AI.method: Advanced fireball models combining general relativistic light bending, polarized transport in magnetized photospheres, magnetic photon splitting attenuation, and magnetospheric vacuum birefringence, applied to confined flux tube geometries with adiabatic fireballs and anisotropic/polarized emergent intensities.
AI.result: Most fireballs are predicted to be highly linearly polarized, especially with vacuum birefringence. Signatures include coexisting direct and lensed delayed images, occultation gaps, and Shapiro+Rømer delay with temporal caustics. Models reproduce double-blackbody SB spectra; the April 2020 SB from SGR 1935+2154 is consistent with a near-pole footpoint and possibly pole-on viewing.
AI.conclusion: The models motivate reverberation-style analyses for SBs and suggest that high-quality data could constrain source geometry, burst crustal footpoints, and potentially neutron star masses and radii.

title: Advancing the detection of low surface brightness galaxies. I. ATTILA: multi-tAsking deTecTIon tool for Lsb gAlaxies
comment: 17 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to A&A Comments are welcome The ATTILA code will be publicly available once the paper has been accepted
summary: Context. Ultra-diffuse galaxies (UDGs) lie at the extreme end of the size-luminosity distribution of low surface-brightness (LSB) galaxies. Their detection and characterization require deep imaging and reliable source detection techniques that can handle low signal-to-noise ratios and severe source blending. Aims. We aim at improving the detection and characterization of the LSB galaxies and UDG candidates in different environments. To this end, we have developed a new automated detection Python-based tool, named ATTILA. Methods. We use deep g- and r-band imaging from the VST Early-type GAlaxy Survey (VEGAS), covering the central region of Hydra I and three new additional fields. Sources are identified combining tiling processing, source detection, and iterative deblending. The structural parameters are derived through surface brightness profile analysis and Sérsic modelling. Cluster membership is determined using the early-type galaxies colour-magnitude relation. Results. We identify 24 new UDGs, doubling the known population in the Hydra-I cluster to 48, consistent with expectations from halo mass scaling relations, and 92 additional LSB galaxies. In real data, ATTILA recovers more than 80% of previously known LSB galaxies and significantly improves the automated detection rate relative to standard methods. Conclusions. By improving the recovery of faint and diffuse sources while mitigating blending and contamination effects, ATTILA enables a more complete census of the LSB galaxy population, including UDGs.

AI.tldr: ATTILA is a new automated Python tool for detecting ultra-diffuse galaxies (UDGs) and low surface-brightness (LSB) galaxies in deep VST/VEGAS imaging. Applied to the Hydra I cluster, it identifies 24 new UDGs (doubling the known population to 48) and 92 LSB galaxies, recovering >80% of previously known LSBs and improving automated detection rates over standard methods.
AI.motivation: Improve detection and characterization of LSB galaxies and UDG candidates in different environments, which have extremely faint signals and severe blending issues that standard techniques struggle with.
AI.method: Developed ATTILA, a Python-based automated detection tool that combines tiling processing, source detection, and iterative deblending. Structural parameters are derived via surface brightness profile analysis and Sérsic modelling, with cluster membership determined using the early-type galaxy colour-magnitude relation. Applied to deep g- and r-band VEGAS imaging covering the Hydra I cluster center plus three new fields.
AI.result: Identified 24 new UDGs (doubling Hydra I's known population to 48), consistent with halo mass scaling relations, plus 92 additional LSB galaxies. ATTILA recovers >80% of previously known LSB galaxies and significantly improves automated detection rates compared to standard methods.
AI.conclusion: By improving recovery of faint and diffuse sources while reducing blending and contamination, ATTILA enables a more complete census of the LSB galaxy population, including UDGs.

title: Seyfert galaxy targets for KM3NeT neutrino telescope
summary: Neutrino signal from a population of Seyfert galaxies has been detected by IceCube neutrino telescope in the muon neutrino channel that has sensitivity mostly to the Northern Hemisphere sources. This detection can be verified by KM3NeT telescope that has sensitivity also in the Southern Hemisphere. We define a catalog of Seyfert galaxies that are expected to be detectable with KM3NeT, assuming that the neutrino luminosity scales with the intrinsic hard X-ray luminosity of the sources. We find that four sources: NGC 1068, NGC 4151, NGC 4945 and Circinus galaxy, are detectable by KM3NeT, if their spectra follow either NGC 1068 or NGC 4151 spectral template based on IceCube data. We discuss uncertainties of the neutrino flux estimate, considering the Compton-thick nature of three of the four detectable sources: NGC 1068, NGC 4945 and Circinus. The limited catalog of the four sources can be used in KM3NeT source search to reduce the trial factor of analysis aimed at independent verification of the neutrino signal from Seyfert galaxies.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies four Seyfert galaxies (NGC 1068, NGC 4151, NGC 4945, Circinus) detectable by KM3NeT, based on IceCube's muon neutrino detection of Seyfert galaxies, aiming to independently verify the neutrino signal using a reduced trial factor analysis.
AI.motivation: To enable independent verification of IceCube's detection of neutrino signal from Seyfert galaxies using KM3NeT, which has complementary sensitivity in the Southern Hemisphere.
AI.method: A catalog of detectable Seyfert galaxies for KM3NeT is defined by assuming neutrino luminosity scales with intrinsic hard X-ray luminosity. Two spectral templates (based on NGC 1068 and NGC 4151 IceCube data) are used to assess detectability.
AI.result: Four sources (NGC 1068, NGC 4151, NGC 4945, Circinus galaxy) are found detectable by KM3NeT. Three of them (NGC 1068, NGC 4945, Circinus) are Compton-thick, introducing uncertainties in neutrino flux estimates.
AI.conclusion: The limited four-source catalog can be used in KM3NeT source searches to reduce the trial factor, facilitating independent verification of the Seyfert neutrino signal detected by IceCube.

title: JWST Advanced Deep Extragalactic Survey (JADES) Data Release 5: stellar population catalogue for galaxies in GOODS-N and GOODS-S
summary: We present the galaxy stellar population catalogue from the JWST Advanced Deep Extragalactic Survey (JADES) Data Release 5 (DR5), providing homogeneous Bayesian inference of physical galaxy properties in GOODS-N and GOODS-S. Using deep JWST/NIRCam and MIRI imaging combined with ancillary multi-wavelength data, we model the spectral energy distributions of ~500,000 sources with the Prospector framework. Our modelling incorporates flexible non-parametric star-formation histories (SFHs), nebular emission, dust attenuation, metallicities, and mid-infrared AGN and dust emission. We adopt an evolving star-forming main sequence (SFMS) prior for modelling the SFHs, which provides a physically-motivated long-term shape of SFHs while retaining non-parametric flexibility. The prior links stellar mass growth and SFR through the observed redshift-dependent SFMS, shaping the global behaviour of the inferred SFHs but allowing substantial deviations and scatters wherever supported by the data. We derive posterior distributions for stellar masses, SFRs, SFHs, dust attenuation, metallicities, and AGN contributions. The depth and wavelength coverage of JADES enable robust stellar mass measurements down to low-mass limits, as well as improved constraints on recent star-formation activity for ~350,000 galaxies at z = 1 - 9. The adoption of a physically motivated prior mitigates unphysical solutions and reduces degeneracies between redshift, age, dust, and metallicity, particularly for faint sources. We validate the catalogue through consistency checks and comparison to spectroscopic redshifts where available. The resulting value-added catalogue provides a uniform set of stellar population parameters suitable for statistical studies of galaxy growth, quenching, and the build-up of stellar mass across cosmic time. The full catalogue and posterior summaries are publicly released as part of JADES DR5.

AI.tldr: The JADES DR5 galaxy stellar population catalogue provides Bayesian-derived physical properties (stellar masses, SFRs, SFHs, dust, metallicity, AGN) for ~500,000 sources in GOODS-N and GOODS-S using JWST/NIRCam+MIRI data and the Prospector framework, with an evolving star-forming main sequence prior that mitigates degeneracies and improves constraints especially for faint, high-redshift galaxies.
AI.motivation: To produce a homogeneous, publicly available catalogue of galaxy stellar population parameters from deep JWST imaging in JADES, enabling statistical studies of galaxy formation and evolution across cosmic time.
AI.method: Spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting with the Prospector framework applied to ~500,000 sources, using flexible non-parametric SFHs, nebular emission, dust attenuation, metallicity, and AGN/dust mid-IR emission, combined with an evolving star-forming main sequence (SFMS) prior that links stellar mass growth and SFR via the observed redshift-dependent SFMS.
AI.result: Robust stellar mass measurements down to low-mass limits and improved constraints on recent star-formation activity for ~350,000 galaxies at z=1–9. The SFMS prior reduces degeneracies (redshift, age, dust, metallicity) and unphysical solutions. The catalogue is validated against spectroscopic redshifts and consistency checks.
AI.conclusion: The catalogue provides a uniform set of stellar population parameters suitable for statistical studies of galaxy growth, quenching, and stellar mass assembly. The full catalogue and posterior summaries are publicly released as part of JADES DR5.

title: Milky Way Mapper decoded abundances -- II: From patterns to paths
summary: The element abundances of Milky Way disc stars encode entangled imprints of multiple enrichment processes, making it difficult to uncover the underlying chemical evolution. Here we re-project 16 stellar abundances for 199,290 red giant stars ([Fe/H]$ > -1$) into a set of (4) shared enrichment patterns, providing a generative framework for learning the organising structure of the Milky Way disc. The relative contributions of these patterns vary systematically across the disc, revealing a low-dimensional enrichment basis that responds coherently to global drivers of disc evolution. By grouping stars according to their pattern contributions, we identify coherent enrichment pathways that exhibit strong chemo-spatial correlations and are stratified in both age and height above the plane, linking radial growth to vertical disc structure. Stars occupying similar positions along these enrichment pathways also show coherent vertical deviations across radius, indicating that the low-dimensional chemical structure captures the disc's response to dynamical perturbations. We identify a transition in enrichment behaviour at approximately 6 Gyr, marking the onset of a more chemically mixed regime with increasing contributions from delayed sources. Within this connected system, the observed $α$-bimodality arises within a shared, low-dimensional abundance structure, with stars populating continuous sequences of changing enrichment fractions that are tightly coupled to spatial, temporal, and orbital coordinates across the Milky Way disc.

AI.tldr: The study re-projects 16 stellar abundances from 199,290 red giant stars into 4 shared enrichment patterns, revealing a low-dimensional structure that organizes Milky Way disc chemical evolution. These patterns show systematic variations across the disc, correlate with age and height, capture dynamical perturbations, and identify a chemical transition at ~6 Gyr—explaining observed α-bimodality within a unified framework.
AI.motivation: Element abundances of Milky Way disc stars encode entangled enrichment processes, making it difficult to uncover underlying chemical evolution. The authors aim to disentangle these signals and reveal the organizing structure of disc chemical evolution.
AI.method: The authors re-project 16 stellar abundances (for 199,290 red giants with [Fe/H] > -1) into a set of 4 shared enrichment patterns using a generative framework, then group stars by pattern contributions to identify enrichment pathways correlated with spatial, temporal, and orbital coordinates.
AI.result: The enrichment patterns vary systematically across the disc, showing strong chemo-spatial correlations stratified by age and height above the plane. A transition in enrichment behaviour at ~6 Gyr marks the onset of a more chemically mixed regime. The observed α-bimodality arises within this low-dimensional structure as continuous sequences of changing enrichment fractions.
AI.conclusion: The low-dimensional chemical structure of the Milky Way disc captures both enrichment history and dynamical perturbations, linking radial growth to vertical disc structure within a connected, coherent framework.

title: Pulsar timing solutions for 17 pulsars at 150~MHz from the Irish LOFAR station
comment: Published in the Open Journal of Astrophysics
summary:
Pulsar timing is a foundational part of pulsar research to triage the most interesting systems and to characterise properties (rotational or otherwise) of the population of these extreme objects. Due to the efficiency of a number of sensitive and/or wide-field surveys in recent years, the number of new pulsars discoveries is growing year-on-year, and most of these lack even basic timing parameter measurements. This work aims to demonstrate the capabilities of international Low Frequency Array (LOAFR) stations operating as single telescopes to follow-up, time and characterise these sources, offering new insight into the emission properties of these neutron stars, and support efforts to build timing models for these sources.
  Between 2020 and 2023 we used the local-mode allocation of the Irish LOFAR station to follow-up 33 pulsar candidates announced from various surveys at different observing frequencies to determine if an international LOFAR station has sufficient sensitivity to detect and time these sources. From the 33 pulsars selected, 22 pulsars were detected and 17 were selected for long-term monitoring across 590 hours of observing time. This has resulted in coherent timing solutions for all of these sources at 150 MHz -- 7 of these have never had any reported timing solutions, the remaining 10 solutions agree well with announcements from others since the beginning of our project. For a fraction of sources announced by surveys each year, the 14 international LOFAR stations are well placed to follow-up survey candidates for long-term pulsar monitoring beyond the standard timing campaigns performed at these telescopes to date, reducing the pressure on observing time availability at these observatories, and enabling the full scientific potential of these pulsars to be realised.

AI.tldr: Using the Irish LOFAR station in local mode (2020-2023), the authors followed up 33 pulsar candidates, detected 22, and obtained coherent timing solutions at 150 MHz for 17 pulsars (7 for the first time), demonstrating that international LOFAR stations can effectively supplement pulsar timing efforts.
AI.motivation: The growing number of pulsar discoveries from sensitive surveys far exceeds the capacity for basic timing parameter measurements, creating a need for additional follow-up resources to characterize these sources.
AI.method: Local-mode observations with the Irish LOFAR station (2020-2023), totaling 590 hours, targeting 33 pulsar candidates detected by various surveys at different observing frequencies.
AI.result: 22/33 pulsars detected; 17 selected for long-term monitoring; coherent timing solutions obtained at 150 MHz for all 17 — 7 of which had no prior timing solutions, and 10 consistent with independently reported solutions.
AI.conclusion: International LOFAR stations are well-suited for follow-up and long-term timing of survey-discovered pulsars, easing demand on primary observatories and enabling fuller scientific exploitation of these sources.

title: Powerful Radio Sources in the Southern Sky. IV. Observations of the G4Jy-3CRE Catalog with the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder
summary: A recent 2023 paper by Massaro et al. introduced the G4Jy-3CRE, a new catalog of the brightest radio sources in the southern hemisphere that serve as a southern equivalent to the Third Cambridge Catalog Revised (3CR). The G4Jy-3CRE catalog selected 264 sources from the GLEAM-4Jy survey based on the same criteria used to select the sources in the 3CR. In this paper, we present new Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP) continuuum imaging of the G4Jy-3CRE catalog. We use the three most recent data releases from the Rapid ASKAP Continuum Survey (RACS), covering the sky south of +30°decl.: RACS-low1, RACS-mid, and RACS-high. Together, these data releases cover a range of frequencies from 600 to 1800 MHz. The RACS surveys have improved spatial resolution and sensitivity over archival surveys at the same frequency, enabling us to classify 173 sources (66% of the sample) with morphologies indicative of the presence of jets, 37 of which did not show jet activity on archival radio maps. We were able to effectively classify FRI/FRII galaxies up to a redshift of z = 1.35. Moreover, we identified six optical counterparts for sources that were either previously unidentified or ambiguous.

AI.tldr: This paper presents new ASKAP continuum imaging of the G4Jy-3CRE catalog (264 bright southern radio sources), using RACS survey data (600-1800 MHz). The improved resolution and sensitivity enabled classification of 173 sources (66%) with jet-related morphologies, including 37 newly identified as jet-active. FRI/FRII classification was possible up to z=1.35, and six new optical counterparts were identified.
AI.motivation: To provide high-resolution, sensitive ASKAP continuum imaging of the G4Jy-3CRE catalog—a southern-hemisphere equivalent to the 3CR catalog—and to improve morphological classification and optical identification of these bright radio sources.
AI.method: Imaging the G4Jy-3CRE catalog (264 sources from GLEAM-4Jy) using the three latest RACS data releases (RACS-low1, RACS-mid, RACS-high) across 600-1800 MHz, covering the sky south of +30° declination.
AI.result: Classified 173 sources (66%) with jet-indicative morphologies, 37 of which were newly identified as jet-active; achieved FRI/FRII classification up to z=1.35; identified six previously unknown or ambiguous optical counterparts.
AI.conclusion: ASKAP's improved resolution and sensitivity over archival surveys significantly advances the morphological classification and optical identification of southern bright radio sources, demonstrating the value of modern radio surveys for extending legacy catalogs.

title: JWST observations of a planetary nebula support jet-driven explosion of core-collapse supernova remnant RCW 103
comment: It will be submitted in two days to allow for comments (including missing references)
summary: We show that the morphology of the core-collapse supernova (CCSN) remnant RCW 103 is very similar to the morphology of the brightest regions in the recently released JWST IR images of the jet-shaped planetary nebula (PN) PMR 1, and conclude that two energetic pairs of jets shaped RCW 103, compatible with the jittering-jets explosion mechanism (JJEM). The PN PMR 1 IR image exhibits two opposite, large, and prominent ears with a narrow, faint region connecting them through the center, a pipe. Observations and simulations have shown that a pair of jets inflates such a pair of ears in PNe. The brightest regions of PN PMR 1 form two clumpy sectors, each shaped like a wide pizza slice, with a faint region between them; the CCSN remnant RCW 103 has a very similar morphology. We identify two shells in the X-ray image of RCW 103 and suggest that two close pairs of energetic jets shaped this CCSN remnant. We find only traces of two of the four expected ears in RCW 103. The ears in RCW 103 were already dispersed and are very faint. Deeper X-ray observations might detect them. Such energetically misaligned pairs of jets are compatible with the JJEM, which predicts that a few to about 20 pairs of jets are responsible for most CCSN explosions.

AI.tldr: The paper shows morphological similarities between CCSN remnant RCW 103 and PN PMR 1's JWST IR image, proposing that two pairs of energetic jets shaped RCW 103 under the jittering-jets explosion mechanism (JJEM).
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that the morphology of CCSN remnant RCW 103 resembles the jet-shaped PN PMR 1, supporting the jittering-jets explosion mechanism (JJEM) as the driver of core-collapse supernova explosions.
AI.method: Comparative morphological analysis between JWST IR images of PN PMR 1 and X-ray images of CCSN remnant RCW 103, identifying shell structures, ear features, and clumpy sectors.
AI.result: Two shells and only traces of two of four expected ears are found in RCW 103; the morphology closely matches PMR 1's clumpy, pizza-slice-shaped sectors with a faint connecting pipe.
AI.conclusion: Two energetically misaligned pairs of jets shaped RCW 103, consistent with JJEM predictions that multiple jet pairs drive most CCSN explosions; deeper X-ray observations may detect the two missing dispersed ears.

title: An AGN in the Antennae galaxies ?
summary: Time variability is a strong probe of energetic phenomena which occur at small spatial scales, like Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN). We use ALMA observations at 100 GHz executed over a period of 2.5 months to look for time variability in the Antennae galaxies, a prototypical early stage merger galaxy pair, for which there are no previous signatures of an AGN in the optical, infrared or X-ray. Most 100 GHz detections in the Antennae are spatially extended and associated with star forming regions, but two sources in the southern galaxy NGC 4039 are compact. One of these compact sources, S3, is offset by 1 arcsecond in the northeast direction from the stellar peak of NGC 4039, and marginally resolved at 10 parsec resolution. The other source, S4, is co-spatial with the stellar peak of NGC 4039 and unresolved even at a resolution of 4 parsec. We examine the time variability of these two sources using their power spectrum. We find that S4 varies with a characteristic timescale of 13+/-3 days, indicating that the phenomena responsible for the 100 GHz emission is smaller than 0.01 parsecs. By comparing the observed flux of the two sources with various candidate origins, we show that while S3 can be explained either by a young massive stellar cluster or an AGN, S4 is likely to be an AGN that is possibly Compton-thick.

AI.tldr: Using ALMA 100 GHz observations over 2.5 months, this study identifies two compact sources in the Antennae galaxies (merger pair NGC 4038/4039). One source (S4), co-spatial with the stellar peak of NGC 4039 and unresolved at 4 pc resolution, shows time variability with a characteristic timescale of 13±3 days, indicating an emission region smaller than 0.01 pc. While S3 could be either a young stellar cluster or an AGN, S4 is likely a previously undetected Compton-thick AGN.
AI.motivation: To search for time variability in the Antennae galaxies—a prototypical early-stage merger—where no prior optical, infrared, or X-ray signatures of an AGN have been found, using time variability as a probe for energetic small-scale phenomena like AGN.
AI.method: ALMA observations at 100 GHz over 2.5 months; power spectrum analysis of time variability; comparison of observed flux with candidate origins.
AI.result: Two compact sources (S3, S4) identified in NGC 4039. S4 varies with characteristic timescale 13±3 days, implying emission region <0.01 pc. S3 is marginally resolved at 10 pc; S4 is unresolved at 4 pc resolution.
AI.conclusion: S4 is likely a previously undetected (possibly Compton-thick) AGN; S3 could be a young massive stellar cluster or an AGN. Time variability at 100 GHz can reveal hidden AGN in mergers where other wavelengths show no signatures.

title: Polarized 3D Synthetic Turbulence I: Magnetic Field Line Random Walk
summary: The behavior of magnetic field lines in a turbulent plasma is a key property of the medium, with important consequences for plasma dynamics and charged-particle transport. We study the diffusion properties of magnetic field lines in synthetic turbulence featuring different polarization configurations for the magnetic perturbations, as prescribed by the existing magnetohydrodynamic modes (namely, Alfvénic and magnetosonic). These turbulent field realizations are then compared with the isotropic (or, random) polarization case, which is the one typically adopted in the literature. We construct polarized synthetic turbulence simulations and study the properties of field lines through the running diffusion coefficient. Our key findings can be summarized as follow: (i) field line wandering is strongly dependent on polarization configurations, (ii) we unveil that the sub-diffusive phase of field line is highly dependent on the polarization and is well reproduced by theoretical predictions based on Corrsin's hypothesis in the low turbulence level regime, (iii) in particular the scaling of the asymptotic diffusion coefficient in magnetosonic-like polarization is $(δB/B)^4$ at odd with the $(δB/B)^2$ scaling found in the quasi-linear regime for random polarization, (iv) interestingly we note that the subdiffusive phase of field line transport in the magnetosonic-like polarization follows closely the one observed in recent high resolution MHD turbulence simulations, we end giving a word of caution when FL transport is investigated in such simulations.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how magnetic field line diffusion in turbulent plasmas depends on the polarization of magnetic perturbations (Alfvénic, magnetosonic, and isotropic). Key findings include: field line wandering strongly depends on polarization; the sub-diffusive phase matches Corrsin's hypothesis; magnetosonic polarization yields a (δB/B)^4 scaling for the diffusion coefficient vs. (δB/B)^2 for random polarization; and magnetosonic polarization reproduces subdiffusion seen in high-resolution MHD simulations.
AI.motivation: Magnetic field line behavior in turbulent plasmas is crucial for plasma dynamics and charged-particle transport, but prior work typically assumed isotropic (random) polarization. This paper aims to understand how realistic polarization configurations (Alfvénic and magnetosonic modes) affect field line diffusion compared to the isotropic assumption.
AI.method: The authors construct synthetic turbulence simulations with different polarization configurations prescribed by MHD modes (Alfvénic, magnetosonic, and isotropic/random). They analyze field line transport properties using the running diffusion coefficient and compare results to theoretical predictions based on Corrsin's hypothesis.
AI.result: (i) Field line wandering strongly depends on polarization; (ii) the sub-diffusive phase matches Corrsin's hypothesis at low turbulence; (iii) magnetosonic polarization yields asymptotic diffusion coefficient scaling of (δB/B)^4, differing from the (δB/B)^2 scaling for random polarization; (iv) magnetosonic subdiffusion closely matches recent high-resolution MHD turbulence simulations.
AI.conclusion: Polarization configuration fundamentally affects magnetic field line diffusion, with magnetosonic modes producing significantly different transport scaling than the commonly assumed isotropic case. Caution is warranted when interpreting field line transport in MHD simulations without accounting for polarization effects.

title: Silicate cosmic dust grain collisions in the interstellar medium: A molecular dynamics study
comment: To be submitted to A&A, comments welcome
summary: (abridged) We aim to predict the most important parameters for grain-grain collision outcomes for models of interstellar grain population evolution on astrophysical scales: the threshold velocity above which colliding grains shatter, the threshold for vaporization, and resulting distributions of grain sizes. We use molecular dynamics simulations which evolve the dynamics of each atom in a dust grain to explore the outcomes of collisions between silicate grains of radii $a \in [5,50]~Å$ at velocities $0.1-20$ km/s. We run simulations of grains with two materials: amorphous SiO$_2$ and an amorphous silicate of composition suggested by Draine \& Hensley (2021). With these simulations, we quantify the collision velocity dependence of shattered and vaporized mass fractions, and the resulting size distributions of shattering products. We find grain shattering thresholds are $\sim$6 km/s for both amorphous SiO$_2$ and astrodust material, which is a factor of $\sim$2 higher than the canonical value for silicates of 2.7 km/s from Jones et al. (1996). This discrepancy is mostly alleviated by correcting an error in the expression for these velocity thresholds derived in Tielens et al. (1994). We find that the size distributions of shattered products are generally not consistent with the power law distributions predicted by this previous model. We also find that their expression fails to predict the fraction of shattered or vaporized material observed in our numerical simulations. The model of Hirashita \& Kobayashi (2013) for the same quantities similarly fails to match the simulations. We provide updated shattering velocity thresholds for standard candidate grain materials to the astrophysics community. Broadly, our updated threshold velocities that astrophysical dust grains may be more robust to shattering in the interstellar medium than previously assumed.

AI.tldr: Using molecular dynamics simulations of silicate grain collisions (radii 5–50 Å, velocities 0.1–20 km/s), the authors find shattering thresholds of ~6 km/s for amorphous SiO₂ and astrodust—about 2× higher than the canonical 2.7 km/s from Jones et al. (1996). The discrepancy is largely explained by an error in Tielens et al. (1994). Previous power-law size distributions and shattering/vaporization fraction predictions (Tielens et al. 1994; Hirashita & Kobayashi 2013) do not match the simulations. Updated thresholds are provided, suggesting interstellar grains are more robust to shattering than previously thought.
AI.motivation: To accurately predict key parameters (shattering threshold, vaporization threshold, and size distributions) governing grain-grain collisions in interstellar dust evolution models, as previous analytical models may be inaccurate.
AI.method: Molecular dynamics simulations tracking individual atoms in nanoscale silicate grains (radii 5–50 Å) colliding at velocities 0.1–20 km/s, using both amorphous SiO₂ and a Draine & Hensley (2021) astrodust composition.
AI.result: Shattering thresholds are ~6 km/s for both materials—~2× the canonical 2.7 km/s. Previous models (Tielens et al. 1994; Hirashita & Kobayashi 2013) fail to reproduce the simulated size distributions and mass fractions. The discrepancy with Jones et al. (1996) is largely due to an error in Tielens et al. (1994)'s velocity expression.
AI.conclusion: Updated shattering velocity thresholds are provided; interstellar dust grains may be more resistant to shattering than previously assumed, suggesting revisions to grain population evolution models are needed.

title: Generation of Quantum Turbulence by Neutrino Cooling in Neutron Stars
summary: The interior crust and much of the liquid core of neutron stars is believed to be a quantum liquid mixture of neutron and proton superfluids and a relativistic electron liquid. Quantized vortices in the neutron superfluid and quantized flux lines in the proton superconductor are topological defects of these hadronic condensates. I consider the formation of the superfluid state in young neutron stars under non-equilibrium conditions imposed by the neutrino cooling rate. The nonequilibrium phase transition implies that the onset of superfluidity is accompanied by the generation of quantized vortices based on the mechanism envisioned by Kibble in the context cosmic string formation in an evolutionary models of an expanding universe, and further developed by Zurek for nonequilibrium phase transitions in quantum liquids such as \Hefour. I discuss the Kibble-Zurek mechanism (KZM) and scaling relations for topological defect formation starting from the Cooper pair fluctuation propagator for temperatures approaching $T_c$. I then calculate the predicted vortex densities based on Urca and modified Urca cooling mechanisms in the cores of neutron stars for several models of the superfluid gap and transition temperature of the interior neutron superfluid. In all cases studied the KZM leads to a large density of topological defects in the condensate phase, which in 3D form a random network of vortex lines and loops, i.e. the generation of quantum turbulence.

AI.tldr: This paper applies the Kibble-Zurek mechanism (KZM) to predict the formation of quantized vortices and quantum turbulence in neutron star superfluid interiors during non-equilibrium phase transitions driven by neutrino cooling, calculating vortex densities based on Urca cooling models and superfluid gap parameters.
AI.motivation: To understand the formation of topological defects (vortices, flux lines) in neutron star superfluids under non-equilibrium conditions imposed by neutrino cooling, extending cosmological defect formation concepts to astrophysical condensed matter systems.
