AI.method: Analytical calculation using the Kibble-Zurek mechanism and Cooper pair fluctuation propagator near Tc, combined with Urca and modified Urca cooling rates for neutron star cores, applied to various superfluid gap models and transition temperatures.
AI.result: The KZM predicts a large density of topological defects in all studied cases, forming a random 3D network of vortex lines and loops—i.e., quantum turbulence—in the neutron superfluid condensate.
AI.conclusion: Non-equilibrium superfluid formation in young neutron stars leads to significant quantum turbulence via the Kibble-Zurek mechanism, with defect densities calculable from cooling and gap model parameters.

title: MICONIC: The multiphase circumnuclear region of Centaurus A as seen with JWST/MIRI MRS observations. I. Spectral inventory and properties of the warm molecular disk
summary: Supermassive black holes power Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN), injecting energy that regulates accretion and shapes host galaxies. We investigate the morphology, excitation, and kinematics of molecular hydrogen (H2) in the inner circumnuclear disk of Centaurus A, the nearest radio galaxy. We present JWST/MIRI MRS integral-field spectroscopy of the central 170x100 pc2 at 0.3"-0.7" (5-12 pc) resolution, focusing on pure rotational H2 lines. The spectra show strong nuclear continuum and bright H2 emission from S(1) to S(8), including the first S(8) detection in Centaurus A. Optically thin nuclear lines enable maps of temperature, column density, and ortho-to-para ratio from spaxel-level excitation-diagram fitting. Warm H2 shows a complex morphology, dominating the central region where CO emission is weak or undetected. Low-excitation H2 lines trace an inhomogeneous ring with a 20-pc-radius cavity aligned with the jet's near side, suggesting that the jet affects the morphology of the molecular disk. Higher-excitation lines form filamentary structures around the AGN. Kinematics are rotational with an S-shaped distortion, indicating non-circular motions or a warped disk. A coherent, low-dispersion (70 km/s) streamer spirals inward. A power-law temperature distribution yields a warm (100-2000 K) H2 mass of (5.6+/-1.4)e5 Msun and a dynamical mass of 5e8 Msun within 100 pc. Shock excitation is supported by enhanced H2/continuum and H2/PAH ratios, elevated [Ne III]/[Ne II], and sub-equilibrium ortho-to-para ratios (1.6-2.4). Turbulent dissipation can balance H2 cooling and likely dominates heating beyond 30 pc. In the inner 100 pc of Centaurus A, AGN feeding and feedback are linked: shocks excite H2, regulate the gas temperature, and prevent cooling below 100 K, explaining the weak CO emission and lack of a massive outflow. These shocks may drive angular momentum loss and help fuel the nucleus.

AI.tldr: JWST/MIRI MRS observations of Centaurus A's inner 170x100 pc reveal warm H₂ morphology, kinematics, and excitation. Shock excitation dominates, regulating gas temperature and preventing cooling, which explains weak CO emission and links AGN feeding/feedback.
AI.motivation: To understand how AGN feedback regulates accretion and shapes host galaxies by investigating the molecular gas properties in the nearest radio galaxy, Centaurus A.
AI.method: JWST/MIRI MRS integral-field spectroscopy at 0.3"-0.7" (5-12 pc) resolution, covering pure rotational H₂ lines S(1) to S(8) in the central 170x100 pc². Spaxel-level excitation-diagram fitting for temperature, column density, and ortho-to-para ratio maps.
AI.result: Warm H₂ mass (5.6±1.4)×10⁵ M☉, dynamical mass 5×10⁸ M☉ within 100 pc. Low-excitation lines show an inhomogeneous ring with a 20-pc cavity aligned with the jet. Ortho-to-para ratios (1.6-2.4) indicate sub-equilibrium. Enhanced H₂/continuum, H₂/PAH ratios, and elevated [Ne III]/[Ne II] support shock excitation. Turbulent dissipation dominates heating beyond 30 pc.
AI.conclusion: In the inner 100 pc of Centaurus A, shocks excite H₂, regulate gas temperature, and prevent cooling below 100 K, explaining weak CO emission and lack of massive outflow. These shocks may drive angular momentum loss and help fuel the AGN, linking feeding and feedback processes.

title: The habitability trade-off: Chemical decoupling and quenching in massive galaxies
comment: accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Massive galaxies experience complex evolutionary processes, including mergers and gas accretion, which can disrupt the chemical equilibrium between their stellar and gaseous components. Using the IllustrisTNG (TNG100) simulation at $z=0$, we investigated the prevalence and physical properties of such chemically decoupled systems within the massive star-forming galaxy population. We identify a substantial subpopulation ($\sim 31.5\%$ of the sample) that exhibits systematic stellar-gas decoupling, characterised by a metal-rich stellar component coexisting with a diluted gas reservoir. These non-equilibrium galaxies are closely linked to recent merger activity and partial quenching, and display systematically suppressed star-formation rates and reduced gas fractions, consistent with a transitional evolutionary phase. We then examined the implications of this phase for galaxy-scale habitability prescriptions by applying a terrestrial planet abundance proxy that combines stellar mass, gas-phase metallicity, and the rate of sterilising events. Despite their diluted gas reservoirs, non-equilibrium galaxies dominate the high end of the inferred present-day habitability proxy distribution, exceeding equilibrium systems by more than an order of magnitude. We interpret this as a habitability trade-off: the same gas dilution and quenching processes that reduce the efficiency of future terrestrial planet formation simultaneously create a transient phase of suppressed radiation hazards for existing planets. The Andromeda galaxy (M31) shows qualitative similarities to this chemically decoupled population, suggesting that galaxies exiting their peak star-forming phase represent a distinct and highly relevant demographic for galaxy-scale habitability. Galactic habitability is therefore intrinsically time-dependent.

AI.tldr: Using TNG100 simulations, ~31.5% of massive star-forming galaxies at z=0 show chemical decoupling (metal-rich stars + diluted gas), linked to mergers and partial quenching. These galaxies dominate the high end of present-day habitability proxies despite suppressed star formation, revealing a time-dependent trade-off in galactic habitability.
AI.motivation: Massive galaxies undergo mergers and gas accretion that can disrupt chemical equilibrium between stars and gas. The prevalence and properties of such chemically decoupled systems, and their implications for galaxy-scale habitability, were poorly understood.
AI.method: Analyzed the IllustrisTNG (TNG100) simulation at z=0, identifying chemically decoupled massive star-forming galaxies via stellar-gas metallicity discrepancies. Applied a terrestrial planet abundance proxy combining stellar mass, gas-phase metallicity, and sterilizing event rates to assess habitability implications.
AI.result: ~31.5% of galaxies exhibit systematic stellar-gas decoupling. These non-equilibrium galaxies are linked to mergers and partial quenching, with suppressed SFRs and gas fractions. They dominate the high-end habitability proxy distribution, exceeding equilibrium systems by >10x.
AI.conclusion: Galactic habitability is intrinsically time-dependent. A transient phase exists where gas dilution and quenching reduce future planet formation efficiency but simultaneously suppress radiation hazards for existing planets. M31 shows qualitative similarity, indicating galaxies exiting peak star formation are a key demographic for habitability studies.

title: Probing the ion-neutral drift velocity towards the L1544 prestellar core: Detection of ambipolar diffusion using N$_2$D$^+$ and para-NH$_2$D
comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: The dynamical role of the magnetic field in the star formation process is tightly linked to the coupling between matter and the field. This coupling is due to the interaction between ions and neutrals in the partially ionized interstellar medium. When the ionization degree drops in the dense environment of prestellar cores, the magnetic field and the matter may decouple, leading to differences in the infalling velocities of ions and neutrals known as ambipolar diffusion. The onset of gravitational collapse resulting from ion-neutral decoupling has never been observed. The aim of this work is to search for signatures of ambipolar diffusion within a prestellar core. We observed the deuterated N$_2$D$^+$ ion and the neutral para-NH$_2$D species towards the prototypical prestellar core L1544. These two species are ideal tracers of prestellar cores sampling the same high densities in the core interior. We compared the velocity centroid and linewidth maps of the ion-neutral pair. We find a mean ion-neutral velocity difference of $\sim$0.05 km/s towards the core. By comparing with predictions from self-consistent calculations of the ambipolar resistivity including dust grain growth, we interpret the observed ion-neutral velocity difference in L1544 as a signature of ambipolar diffusion. We do not detect a significant ion-neutral linewidth difference that may be attributed to the subsonic infall motions of the gas in L1544 and geometrical effects in the presence of inclination. These results emphasize the role of dust grain growth at the prestellar core stage in setting the ambipolar resistivity and regulating the dynamical evolution of dense cores towards their collapse into protostars. We propose that measurements of ion-neutral drift velocities provide new constraints on the total magnetic field strength and the dust size distribution within prestellar cores.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the first observational signature of ambipolar diffusion in the prestellar core L1544, detected by comparing velocity centroids of the ion N₂D⁺ and neutral para-NH₂D, finding an ion-neutral velocity difference of ~0.05 km/s interpreted as evidence of ion-neutral decoupling, and highlighting the role of dust grain growth in setting ambipolar resistivity.
AI.motivation: The onset of gravitational collapse resulting from ion-neutral decoupling (ambipolar diffusion) in prestellar cores has never been observed. This work aims to search for observational signatures of ambipolar diffusion within the prototypical prestellar core L1544.
AI.method: Observations of the deuterated ion N₂D⁺ and the neutral species para-NH₂D toward L1544 were conducted. Velocity centroid and linewidth maps of this ion-neutral pair were compared, along with comparisons to self-consistent calculations of ambipolar resistivity including dust grain growth.
AI.result: A mean ion-neutral velocity difference of ~0.05 km/s was detected toward the core, interpreted as a signature of ambipolar diffusion. No significant ion-neutral linewidth difference was found, attributed to subsonic infall motions and geometrical effects with inclination.
AI.conclusion: These results emphasize the role of dust grain growth at the prestellar core stage in setting ambipolar resistivity and regulating dynamical evolution. Measurements of ion-neutral drift velocities provide new constraints on total magnetic field strength and dust size distribution within prestellar cores.

title: Dwarf Galaxy Constraints on Interacting Fermionic Dark Matter
summary: Dwarf galaxies in the Local Group offer a way to test dark matter (DM) models against stellar kinematic data. In this work, we study degenerate fermionic DM in two cases: the standard non-interacting Fermi gas, and an interacting degenerate DM fluid described by a phenomenological equation of state motivated by interacting Fermi systems. These interactions modify the compressibility of the DM fluid and, in some regions of parameter space, lead to mechanically unstable branches that must be treated through a Maxwell construction. We solve the corresponding non-relativistic hydrostatic equations consistently and compute the line-of-sight velocity-dispersion profiles using the spherical Jeans equation. We then perform MCMC fits to eight classical Milky Way dwarf spheroidal galaxies. The data favor DM fermion masses in the range $100$--$300\,{\rm eV}$. We find that the interacting and non-interacting equations of state give broadly similar posterior distributions for the fermion mass, central density, and stellar anisotropy. Current data therefore do not strongly prefer an interacting equation of state over the free degenerate Fermi-gas, thereby excluding large deviations from the non-interacting limit.

AI.tldr: The paper tests degenerate fermionic dark matter models (non-interacting vs. interacting) against kinematic data from eight classical Milky Way dwarf spheroidal galaxies, finding that both models yield similar mass constraints (~100-300 eV) and that current data do not strongly favor interacting over non-interacting DM.
AI.motivation: To test dark matter models using stellar kinematic data from Local Group dwarf galaxies, specifically comparing non-interacting and interacting degenerate fermionic DM scenarios.
AI.method: Solved non-relativistic hydrostatic equations with Maxwell construction for unstable branches, computed line-of-sight velocity-dispersion profiles via spherical Jeans equation, and performed MCMC fits to eight classical Milky Way dwarf spheroidal galaxies.
AI.result: DM fermion masses favored in 100-300 eV range; interacting and non-interacting equations of state produce broadly similar posterior distributions for fermion mass, central density, and stellar anisotropy.
AI.conclusion: Current data do not strongly prefer an interacting equation of state over the free degenerate Fermi gas, excluding large deviations from the non-interacting limit.

title: Mass Segregation in the CMZoom Survey
summary: We employ a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) approach to characterize the spatial distribution and mass segregation of compact millimeter continuum sources within the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) of the Milky Way. We use a modified form of the complete version of the 1.3 mm dust continuum catalog from the CMZoom survey, which identifies 685 compact sources with typical effective radii of $\sim0.1$ pc. For 22 of 35 CMZ clouds, we calculate the thermal and turbulent Jeans lengths and masses, and determine that compact source separations, as well as compact source masses, are more consistent with thermal fragmentation at $\sim0.1$ pc size scales. We construct the mass segregation ratios for compact sources in 17 CMZ clouds and determine that 5 of the analyzed clouds display some form of mass segregation ($Λ_{MSR} > 1.5$), while the remaining clouds show either inverse mass segregation ($Λ_{MSR} < 0.75$), or no evidence of true mass segregation ($0.75 < Λ_{MSR} < 1.5$). Finally, we find that although some actively star-forming clouds do exhibit mass segregation, other similarly active clouds do not, indicating an unclear correlation with evolutionary stage for star forming clouds in the CMZ, given the current available data.

AI.tldr: Using a Minimum Spanning Tree approach on 685 compact millimeter sources from the CMZoom survey, we find that source separations and masses in CMZ clouds are consistent with thermal fragmentation at ~0.1 pc scales. Mass segregation analysis shows 5 out of 17 clouds exhibit mass segregation, with no clear correlation to evolutionary stage.
AI.motivation: To characterize the spatial distribution and mass segregation of compact millimeter continuum sources within the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) of the Milky Way, and to understand the fragmentation processes governing star formation in this extreme environment.
AI.method: Applied a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) approach to a modified complete 1.3 mm dust continuum catalog from the CMZoom survey (685 compact sources, typical effective radii ~0.1 pc). Calculated thermal and turbulent Jeans lengths/masses for 22 of 35 CMZ clouds, and constructed mass segregation ratios for compact sources in 17 CMZ clouds.
AI.result: Compact source separations and masses are more consistent with thermal fragmentation at ~0.1 pc scales. Of 17 clouds analyzed, 5 show mass segregation (Λ_MSR > 1.5), while others show inverse segregation (Λ_MSR < 0.75) or no evidence (0.75 < Λ_MSR < 1.5). No clear correlation between mass segregation and evolutionary stage was found.
AI.conclusion: Thermal fragmentation dominates at ~0.1 pc scales in CMZ clouds. Mass segregation is present in some but not all actively star-forming clouds, indicating an unclear correlation with evolutionary stage given current data.

title: From protogalaxy through thick and thin: Why did the Milky Way evolve in three kinematic phases?
summary: APOGEE and Gaia data have revealed that the Milky Way's structure appears to have evolved through three distinct kinematic phases. First, at early cosmic times, the Milky Way was a disordered protogalaxy, which subsequently "spun up" to a second kinematic phase marked by star formation occurring in a rotating, thick stellar disk. The thick disk phase later transitioned to a third (and final) phase with star formation occurring in a cold, thin stellar disk. In this paper, we use a suite of FIRE-2 simulations of Milky Way-mass galaxies to demonstrate that the same three phases arise in our cosmological zoom-in simulations, and study their physical origin. In all of our galaxies, the early disordered phase occurs when the rate of cool gas ($T \leq 10^4$ K) converting into stars is low, the star formation rate is bursty, and the baryonic mass "sloshes" within the host potential with respect to the center of mass motion. The gas in the galaxy begins to spin coherently after the sloshing phase ends, followed by the spin-up of young stars. The central potential of the galaxy is least concentrated just prior to gas spin-up. This second, thick disk phase coincides with a period when the rate of cool gas converting into stars is highest, even though the star formation rate remains bursty in this phase. The final transition to the thin disk phase occurs when the inner circumgalactic medium virializes. The thin disk phase is associated with a time of steady star formation and intermediate rates of cool gas converting into stars. Mergers do not appear to play a defining role in driving transitions between the three phases. The condition for the formation of a thick disk appears to be fairly minimal: a stable center of mass motion. The formation of a thin disk requires more: gas must accrete slowly enough for its angular momentum to mix and become coherent prior to joining the galaxy.

AI.tldr: Using FIRE-2 simulations of Milky Way-mass galaxies, this paper identifies three distinct kinematic phases in Galaxy evolution—disordered protogalaxy, rotating thick disk, and cold thin disk—driven by cool gas conversion rates, star formation burstiness, center-of-mass stability, CGM virialization, and gas accretion coherence, with mergers playing no defining role in phase transitions.
AI.motivation: To understand the physical origin of the three kinematic phases (disordered protogalaxy → thick disk → thin disk) observed in the Milky Way's structure using APOGEE and Gaia data, by testing whether these phases arise in simulations and identifying the underlying physical mechanisms.
AI.method: A suite of FIRE-2 cosmological zoom-in simulations of Milky Way-mass galaxies was analyzed to trace kinematic phases and associated physical conditions: cool gas conversion rate, star formation burstiness, baryonic center-of-mass motion ("sloshing"), potential concentration, CGM virialization, gas angular momentum coherence, and merger activity.
AI.result: All simulated galaxies exhibit the same three phases. The disordered phase coincides with bursty star formation, low cool-gas-to-star conversion, and baryonic sloshing. The thick disk phase begins after sloshing ends, with peak cool gas conversion but still bursty star formation, and the potential is least concentrated just before gas spin-up. The thin disk phase emerges when the inner CGM virializes, with steady star formation and intermediate cool gas conversion rates. Mergers are not the primary drivers of transitions.
AI.conclusion: A stable center-of-mass motion is a minimal condition for thick disk formation, while thin disk formation additionally requires slow gas accretion such that angular momentum can mix and become coherent before gas joins the galaxy. Mergers do not play a defining role in driving phase transitions.
